lead: An IoT architecture is a plan for where data is sensed, moved, stored, processed and used. It breaks a large system into layers with clear jobs, so teams can build and test each part without breaking the rest. The same system can be drawn as three layers, five layers, or a seven-level reference model. This chapter shows those models, places edge, fog and cloud correctly, and gives design principles. It is used when you plan a real deployment, such as thousands of Chennai water meters or a factory sensor network.

blocks.text: An IoT system has many small devices, several networks and many users. Architecture divides the work into layers so each part has one job. A change in a dashboard then does not force a change in a sensor. The three-layer model is the simplest.

items: Perception layer: sensors and actuators touch the physical world. It collects readings and can act.
Network layer: communication modules, gateways and routers move data.
Application layer: software gives reports, alarms and controls to users.

blocks.text: The five-layer model keeps perception at the bottom and application near the top. It calls the second layer transport; this does the work of the network layer. It adds processing in the middle for storage and analysis. It adds business at the top for rules, decisions and value. Business is the top layer only in the five-layer model. Do not mix the layer names of the two models.

The logical design describes functions; a layered architecture arranges those functions into levels. Use the three-layer model for a quick sketch and the five-layer model when storage, analysis or business rules need their own place.

Some syllabi call this an architectural overview; others call it a layered reference model. The seven-level model, often called the IoT World Forum model, gives more detail. Read it from bottom to top.

items: Physical devices and controllers: sensors, actuators and machines that produce data or act.
Connectivity: links, gateways and protocols that carry data.
Edge computing: local processing near devices for filtering, fast alarms and control.
Data accumulation: storage of current and historical data.
Data abstraction: schemas and views that make stored data usable.
Collaboration: people and processes that share results across teams or organisations.

blocks.text: Management and security cut across every level. Management covers device setup, monitoring and updates. Security covers identity, encryption and access control. They are not extra layers. A weak sensor and a weak cloud account are both entry points. Only a few universities teach the seven levels in detail; know the order and the two cross-cutting concerns. The levels are not a protocol stack; they divide responsibilities.

Where processing sits matters. Edge is on or near the device: quick decisions and less traffic. Fog is a local server or gateway cluster: regional storage and analysis. Cloud is central: large storage, long history and many users. A good design pushes only needed data upward. Keep control loops at the edge when delay matters. Cloud and fog implementation is in Unit 5.

items: Scalability: adding devices must not need a redesign.
Modularity: replace one sensor or gateway without rebuilding all.
Interoperability: different vendors' devices exchange data through standard formats.
Security and privacy: protect data and personal information at every layer.
Reliability: keep working when a link fails; use retries and local buffers.
Energy efficiency: send less and sleep more for battery devices.
Open standards: avoid lock-in and make testing easier.

blocks.text: Use these principles to judge an architecture, not just count layers. A design that sends every raw reading to the cloud may be simple but costly at scale.

spec.aria: Three layers stacked: a row of 20 sensors at the bottom sends 20 arrows into the network-layer gateway, which sends one thick arrow up to the application layer; text below gives 4,000 divided by 20 equals 200 uplinks a minute.

examples.question: A three-layer design has 4,000 sensors. Each sensor sends 1 packet per minute. The network layer aggregates 20 packets into one uplink. Find the uplinks per minute.
steps: Packets from one sensor in one minute = 1 packet per minute.
Total packets per minute = 4,000 sensors × 1 packet per minute = 4,000 packets per minute.
Uplinks per minute = 4,000 packets per minute ÷ 20 packets per uplink = 200 uplinks per minute.
examples.answer: The network layer sends 200 uplinks per minute.
examples.check:
sensors = 4000
packets_per_sensor = 1
aggregation = 20
packets = sensors * packets_per_sensor
uplinks = packets / aggregation
print(int(uplinks))

traps: Business is the top layer only in the five-layer model. In the three-layer model the top layer is application.
The second layer is called network in the three-layer model and transport in the five-layer model; they refer to the same data-movement job.
Management and security are cross-cutting concerns in the seven-level model, not extra layers on top.
More layers do not automatically mean a better design. Match the model to the system's real needs.
Aggregating 20 packets into 1 uplink reduces uplinks to 1/20; it does not reduce the packets sent by sensors.

quiz.q: Name the three layers of the three-layer IoT model from bottom to top.
Why does the five-layer model add a processing layer?
quiz.a: It gives storage and analysis their own place, so the network does not carry raw data straight to every application.

quiz.q: What does it mean that security is cross-cutting in the seven-level model?
quiz.a: Security applies at every level, from device identity to cloud access, not as a single separate layer.

quiz.q: A design has 600 sensors. Each sends 1 packet per minute. The network layer aggregates 15 packets into one uplink. Find the uplinks per minute.
quiz.a: Total packets = 600 × 1 = 600 per minute. Uplinks = 600 ÷ 15 = 40 uplinks per minute.

quiz.q: A design has 2,500 sensors. Each sends 2 packets per minute. Aggregation is 25 packets per uplink. Find the uplinks per minute.
quiz.a: Total packets = 2,500 × 2 = 5,000 per minute. Uplinks = 5,000 ÷ 25 = 200 uplinks per minute.

quiz.q: Why should a fast alarm for a gas leak run at the edge rather than only in the cloud?
quiz.a: Edge processing avoids network delay and keeps working when the link is down; the cloud can still store history and send reports.

quiz.q: A team adds many sensors and finds the cloud bill rising. Which design principle was ignored, and what change helps?
quiz.a: Scalability and energy efficiency were ignored. Filter or aggregate at the edge and send only needed data upward.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, architectures are drawn as deployment diagrams that show which function runs on which device, gateway or cloud region. Digital twins and asset administration shells add standard ways to describe a physical thing and its data. Researchers study adaptive placement, where processing moves between edge and cloud as load changes. Search for IoT reference architecture, edge-fog-cloud continuum, and cross-cutting security in layered architectures.
